title: Designing REST APIs around resources, not screens
excerpt: A useful API should model the domain clearly so multiple clients can use it without duplicating business rules.
intro: When an application has a web client and a mobile client, it is tempting to build endpoints around each screen. A more durable starting point is to identify the resources and actions in the domain.

sections.heading: Start with the domain
sections.body: List the things the system manages: users, products, invoices, attendance records or articles. These become the starting point for resource-oriented routes.

sections.heading: Keep business rules on the server
sections.body: The browser and mobile app should present state and collect input. Validation, authorization and important state transitions belong on the server so every client follows the same rules.

sections.heading: Design for more than one client
sections.body: A consistent API contract lets a web interface and a mobile app share backend behavior. It also makes testing and future client development easier.

sections.heading: Make errors predictable
sections.body: Return clear status codes and structured error responses. Predictable failures are part of a good API, not an afterthought.

takeaway: Model the business capability once, then let different interfaces use it.

title: Thinking in payment states, not just a Pay button
excerpt: Invoice and payment interfaces need an explicit model of pending, paid and failed states—especially when a prototype is not yet connected to a live provider.
intro: A payment button is only one moment in a longer workflow. The application also needs to represent what happened after the customer tried to pay.

sections.heading: Separate intent from confirmation
sections.body: A customer clicking Pay does not prove that money moved. The application should wait for a trusted provider confirmation before marking a real invoice as paid.

sections.heading: Define the states
sections.body: A simple prototype may distinguish draft, pending, paid, failed and cancelled. The exact states should match the provider and product requirements.

sections.heading: Keep demo behavior honest
sections.body: A demo can simulate a successful payment to help people understand the experience, but it should be visibly identified as a demo and must not be confused with a live transaction.

sections.heading: Plan for asynchronous updates
sections.body: Production payment systems commonly notify the backend asynchronously. The backend should verify those notifications and update the invoice record safely.

takeaway: A trustworthy payment experience depends on accurate state, not just polished screens.

title: Testing a chess engine beyond whether it compiles
excerpt: A chess engine needs repeatable checks for legal moves, search behavior and playing strength—not only a successful build.
intro: Getting an engine to compile is an important milestone, but it says very little about how reliably it plays. Testing needs to cover both correctness and practical behavior.

sections.heading: Check move correctness
sections.body: Start with positions that have known legal moves and verify that the engine never returns an illegal move.

sections.heading: Use repeatable positions
sections.body: A small set of saved positions makes it easier to compare changes and catch regressions as evaluation and search evolve.

sections.heading: Observe practical play
sections.body: Play games against the engine at different settings. Record obvious weaknesses, opening behavior and decisions that look inconsistent.

sections.heading: Change one thing at a time
sections.body: When a test exposes a weakness, make a focused change and rerun the same checks. That makes improvements easier to understand.

takeaway: A working engine is a starting point; repeatable testing is how it becomes dependable.
